title: Ant Intelligence
bodyParagraphs: When we think of intelligent members of the animal kingdom, the creatures that spring immediately to mind are apes and monkeys. But in fact the social lives of some members of the insect kingdom are sufficiently complex to suggest more than a hint of intelligence.

Among these, the world of the ant has come in for considerable scrutiny lately, and the idea that ants demonstrate sparks of cognition has certainly not been rejected by those involved in these investigations.

Ants store food, repel attackers and use chemical signals to contact one another in case of attack. Such chemical communication can be compared to the human use of visual and auditory channels (as in religious chants, advertising images and jingles, political slogans and martial music) to arouse and propagate moods and attitudes. The biologist Lewis Thomas wrote, ‘Ants are so much like human beings as to be an embarrassment. They farm fungi, raise aphids* as livestock, launch armies to war, use chemical sprays to alarm and confuse enemies, capture slaves, engage in child labour, exchange information ceaselessly. They do everything but watch television.’

However, in ants there is no cultural transmission – everything must be encoded in the genes – whereas in humans the opposite is true. Only basic instincts are carried in the genes of a newborn baby, other skills being learned from others in the community as the child grows up. It may seem that this cultural continuity gives us a huge advantage over ants. They have never mastered fire nor progressed. Their fungus farming and aphid herding crafts are sophisticated when compared to the agricultural skills of humans five thousand years ago but have been totally overtaken by modern human agribusiness.

Or have they? The farming methods of ants are at least sustainable. They do not ruin environments or use enormous amounts of energy. Moreover, recent evidence suggests that the crop farming of ants may be more sophisticated and adaptable than was thought.

Ants were farmers fifty million years before humans were. Ants can’t digest the cellulose in leaves – but some fungi can. The ants therefore cultivate these fungi in their nests, bringing them leaves to feed on, and then use them as a source of food. Farmer ants secrete antibiotics to control other fungi that might act as ‘weeds’, and spread waste to fertilise the crop.

It was once thought that the fungus that ants cultivate was a single type that they had propagated, essentially unchanged from the distant past. Not so. Ulrich Mueller of Maryland and his colleagues genetically screened 862 different types of fungi taken from ants’ nests. These turned out to be highly diverse: it seems that ants are continually domesticating new species. Even more impressively, DNA analysis of the fungi suggests that the ants improve or modify the fungi by regularly swapping and sharing strains with neighbouring ant colonies.

Whereas prehistoric man had no exposure to urban lifestyles – the forcing house of intelligence – the evidence suggests that ants have lived in urban settings for close on a hundred million years, developing and maintaining underground cities of specialised chambers and tunnels.

When we survey Mexico City, Tokyo, Los Angeles, we are amazed at what has been accomplished by humans. Yet Hoelldobler and Wilson’s magnificent work for ant lovers, The Ants, describes a supercolony of the ant Formica yessensis on the Ishikari Coast of Hokkaido. This ‘megalopolis’ was reported to be composed of 360 million workers and a million queens living in 4,500 interconnected nests across a territory of 2.7 square kilometres.

Such enduring and intricately meshed levels of technical achievement outstrip by far anything achieved by our distant ancestors. We hail as masterpieces the cave paintings in southern France and elsewhere, dating back some 20,000 years. Ant societies existed in something like their present form more than seventy million years ago. Beside this, prehistoric man looks technologically primitive. Is this then some kind of intelligence, albeit of a different kind?

Research conducted at Oxford, Sussex and Zürich Universities has shown that when desert ants return from a foraging trip, they navigate by integrating bearings and distances, which they continuously update in their heads. They combine the evidence of visual landmarks with a mental library of local directions, all within a framework which is consulted and updated. So ants can learn too.

And in a twelve-year programme of work, Ryabko and Reznikova have found evidence that ants can transmit very complex messages. Scouts who had located food in a maze returned to mobilise their foraging teams. They engaged in contact sessions, at the end of which the scout was removed in order to observe what her team might do. Often the foragers proceeded to the exact spot in the maze where the food had been. Elaborate precautions were taken to prevent the foraging team using odour clues. Discussion now centres on whether the route through the maze is communicated as a ‘left-right’ sequence of turns or as a ‘compass bearing and distance’ message.

During the course of this exhaustive study, Reznikova has grown so attached to her laboratory ants that she feels she knows them as individuals – even without the paint spots used to mark them. It’s no surprise that Edward Wilson, in his essay, ‘In the company of ants’, advises readers who ask what to do with the ants in their kitchen to: ‘Watch where you step. Be careful of little lives.’

questionGroups.summaryText: Ants have sophisticated methods of farming, including herding livestock and growing crops, which are in many ways similar to those used in human agriculture. The ants cultivate a large number of different species of edible fungi which convert 7 ______ into a form which they can digest. They use their own natural 8 ______ as weed-killers and also use unwanted materials as 9 ______. Genetic analysis shows they constantly upgrade these fungi by developing new species and by 10 ______ species with neighbouring ant colonies. In fact, the farming methods of ants could be said to be more advanced than human agribusiness, since they use 11 ______ methods, they do not affect the 12 ______ and do not waste 13 ______.

answerEvidence.evidence: Such chemical communication can be compared to the human use of visual and auditory channels (as in religious chants, advertising images and jingles, political slogans and martial music) to arouse and propagate moods and attitudes.
answerEvidence.reason: The passage compares the channels but identifies ant communication as chemical and human communication as visual and auditory; they are not the same channels.

distractors.TRUE: A comparison between different channel types does not establish that ants and humans use identical channels.
distractors.NOT GIVEN: Both the ant channel and the contrasted human channels are explicitly identified.

answerEvidence.evidence: Whereas prehistoric man had no exposure to urban lifestyles – the forcing house of intelligence – the evidence suggests that ants have lived in urban settings for close on a hundred million years, developing and maintaining underground cities of specialised chambers and tunnels.
answerEvidence.reason: Calling urban lifestyles the forcing house of intelligence directly presents city life as a factor promoting intelligence.

distractors.FALSE: The passage links urban life positively, not negatively, with the development of intelligence.
distractors.NOT GIVEN: The relationship between urban lifestyles and intelligence is explicitly stated.

answerEvidence.evidence: This ‘megalopolis’ was reported to be composed of 360 million workers and a million queens living in 4,500 interconnected nests across a territory of 2.7 square kilometres.
answerEvidence.reason: The passage quantifies the size of an ant city but never compares how quickly ants and humans build cities.

distractors.TRUE: No construction-speed comparison says ants build large cities faster than humans.
distractors.FALSE: No construction-speed comparison says ants build large cities more slowly than or at the same rate as humans.

answerEvidence.evidence: Research conducted at Oxford, Sussex and Zürich Universities has shown that when desert ants return from a foraging trip, they navigate by integrating bearings and distances, which they continuously update in their heads.
answerEvidence.reason: Integrating and updating bearings and distances corresponds to calculations based on position and distance.

distractors.FALSE: The cited research explicitly says desert ants combine bearing and distance information to navigate.
distractors.NOT GIVEN: Both types of navigational information are directly specified.

answerEvidence.evidence: Elaborate precautions were taken to prevent the foraging team using odour clues.
answerEvidence.reason: The experiment deliberately prevented the team from using smell, contradicting the statement that smell enabled it to find the food.

distractors.TRUE: Odour clues were excluded rather than used successfully.
distractors.NOT GIVEN: The role of smell in the experiment is explicitly described.

answerEvidence.evidence: It’s no surprise that Edward Wilson, in his essay, ‘In the company of ants’, advises readers who ask what to do with the ants in their kitchen to: ‘Watch where you step. Be careful of little lives.’
answerEvidence.reason: The passage reports the essay’s practical advice but does not state the essay’s subject or whether it explores ant communication.

distractors.TRUE: Nothing says that the essay examines ant communication.
distractors.FALSE: Nothing says that the essay excludes or contradicts the subject of ant communication; its full scope is unstated.

answerEvidence.evidence: Ants can’t digest the cellulose in leaves – but some fungi can. The ants therefore cultivate these fungi in their nests, bringing them leaves to feed on, and then use them as a source of food.
answerEvidence.reason: The fungi process cellulose, which ants cannot digest directly, into fungal food that ants can digest.

distractors.A: Aphids are livestock herded by ants, not the leaf substance converted by fungi.
distractors.B: Agricultural is an adjective describing farming and cannot name the substance converted.
distractors.D: Exchanging is a later method of sharing fungal strains, not the material being converted.
distractors.E: Energy is what ant farming avoids wasting, not what fungi convert into digestible form.
distractors.F: Fertilizers describe the use of waste, not the substance digested through fungi.
distractors.G: Food is the resulting role of cultivated fungi, not the indigestible input they convert.
distractors.H: Fungi perform the conversion and are eaten; they are not the substance being converted.
distractors.I: Growing describes crop cultivation and cannot fill the noun slot after convert.
distractors.J: Interbreeding is not stated as the material that fungi convert.
distractors.K: Natural is adjectival and supplies neither the required substance nor the correct grammar.
distractors.L: Other species are domesticated or exchanged, not converted into digestible form.
distractors.M: Secretions are used to control weeds, not converted by edible fungi.
distractors.N: Sustainable describes the farming methods and is not a convertible substance.
distractors.O: The environment is protected by ant farming and is not converted into food.

answerEvidence.evidence: Farmer ants secrete antibiotics to control other fungi that might act as ‘weeds’, and spread waste to fertilise the crop.
answerEvidence.reason: The ants’ own antibiotic secretions control competing fungi and therefore function as natural weed-killers.

distractors.A: Aphids are livestock and are not the ants’ weed-killing substance.
distractors.B: Agricultural describes farming and does not name something the ants naturally produce.
distractors.C: Cellulose is the indigestible leaf material processed by fungi, not a weed-killer.
distractors.D: Exchanging describes sharing fungal strains and cannot name a natural substance.
distractors.E: Energy is conserved by ant farming rather than used as a weed-killer.
distractors.F: Fertilizers are the role played by waste, whereas the weed-killer is an antibiotic secretion.
distractors.G: Food is obtained from fungi and is not used to kill weeds.
distractors.H: Fungi are the crop and competing organisms; they are not the ants’ natural weed-killing output.
distractors.I: Growing is an activity, not a natural substance used as a weed-killer.
distractors.J: Interbreeding is not described as a weed-control method.
distractors.K: Natural would produce the impossible repetition “their own natural natural” and does not name the substance.
distractors.L: Other species are not used as weed-killers.
distractors.N: Sustainable describes farming methods and does not name a secretion.
distractors.O: The environment is protected, not applied as a weed-killer.

answerEvidence.evidence: Farmer ants secrete antibiotics to control other fungi that might act as ‘weeds’, and spread waste to fertilise the crop.
answerEvidence.reason: Unwanted waste is spread to fertilise the crop, so it functions as fertilizers.

distractors.A: Aphids are raised as livestock, not used as fertilizing waste.
distractors.B: Agricultural is an adjective and cannot name what unwanted materials become.
distractors.C: Cellulose is leaf material fed to fungi, not the function of discarded material.
distractors.D: Exchanging is the transfer of strains, not a use for waste.
distractors.E: Energy is not the unwanted material spread on the crop.
distractors.G: Food is produced from fungi, whereas the unwanted material enriches the crop.

distractors.L: Other species are domesticated or exchanged, not used as waste products.

answerEvidence.evidence: Even more impressively, DNA analysis of the fungi suggests that the ants improve or modify the fungi by regularly swapping and sharing strains with neighbouring ant colonies.
answerEvidence.reason: Swapping and sharing strains with neighbouring colonies is paraphrased by exchanging species.

distractors.A: Aphids are livestock and are not the fungal species shared between colonies.
distractors.B: Agricultural is adjectival and cannot describe the transfer action after “by”.
distractors.C: Cellulose is processed by fungi, not exchanged as species with colonies.
distractors.E: Energy is conserved and is not the action used to upgrade fungi.
distractors.F: Fertilizers describe waste use and not the sharing of fungal strains.
distractors.G: Food is the product of fungal cultivation, not the transfer action.
distractors.H: Fungi names the crop but does not supply the required -ing action.
distractors.I: Growing new species is already expressed by “developing new species”; the separate evidence is swapping and sharing them.
distractors.J: Interbreeding would mean breeding strains together, but the passage states swapping and sharing between colonies.
distractors.K: Natural is an adjective and cannot fill the -ing verb slot.
distractors.L: Other species is a noun phrase and cannot fill the action slot or express transfer.
distractors.M: Secretions are antibiotics and are not exchanged species.
distractors.N: Sustainable characterises farming methods rather than fungal exchange.
distractors.O: The environment is protected, not exchanged between colonies.

answerEvidence.evidence: The farming methods of ants are at least sustainable.

distractors.A: Aphids are livestock and cannot describe farming methods.
distractors.B: Agricultural methods is grammatical but merely means farming methods; it does not express the advantage identified in the passage.
distractors.C: Cellulose is a substance and cannot characterise the methods.
distractors.D: Exchanging describes one fungal-management action, not the overall environmental quality of the methods.
distractors.E: Energy is a noun and is something not wasted, not a description of the methods.

distractors.M: Secretions are used as weed control and do not characterise the whole farming system.

READING PASSAGE 1

You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1–13, which are based on Reading Passage 1 below.

Ant Intelligence

When we think of intelligent members of the animal kingdom, the creatures that spring immediately to mind are apes and monkeys. But in fact the social lives of some members of the insect kingdom are sufficiently complex to suggest more than a hint of intelligence.

Among these, the world of the ant has come in for considerable scrutiny lately, and the idea that ants demonstrate sparks of cognition has certainly not been rejected by those involved in these investigations.

Ants store food, repel attackers and use chemical signals to contact one another in case of attack. Such chemical communication can be compared to the human use of visual and auditory channels (as in religious chants, advertising images and jingles, political slogans and martial music) to arouse and propagate moods and attitudes. The biologist Lewis Thomas wrote, ‘Ants are so much like human beings as to be an embarrassment. They farm fungi, raise aphids* as livestock, launch armies to war, use chemical sprays to alarm and confuse enemies, capture slaves, engage in child labour, exchange information ceaselessly. They do everything but watch television.’

However, in ants there is no cultural transmission – everything must be encoded in the genes – whereas in humans the opposite is true. Only basic instincts are carried in the genes of a newborn baby, other skills being learned from others in the community as the child grows up. It may seem that this cultural continuity gives us a huge advantage over ants. They have never mastered fire nor progressed. Their fungus farming and aphid herding crafts are sophisticated when compared to the agricultural skills of humans five thousand years ago but have been totally overtaken by modern human agribusiness.

Or have they? The farming methods of ants are at least sustainable. They do not ruin environments or use enormous amounts of energy. Moreover, recent evidence suggests that the crop farming of ants may be more sophisticated and adaptable than was thought.

Ants were farmers fifty million years before humans were. Ants can’t digest the cellulose in leaves – but some fungi can. The ants therefore cultivate these fungi in their nests, bringing them leaves to feed on, and then

* aphids: small insects of a different species from ants
pages.70:
use them as a source of food. Farmer ants secrete antibiotics to control other fungi that might act as ‘weeds’, and spread waste to fertilise the crop.

It was once thought that the fungus that ants cultivate was a single type that they had propagated, essentially unchanged from the distant past. Not so. Ulrich Mueller of Maryland and his colleagues genetically screened 862 different types of fungi taken from ants’ nests. These turned out to be highly diverse: it seems that ants are continually domesticating new species. Even more impressively, DNA analysis of the fungi suggests that the ants improve or modify the fungi by regularly swapping and sharing strains with neighbouring ant colonies.

Whereas prehistoric man had no exposure to urban lifestyles – the forcing house of intelligence – the evidence suggests that ants have lived in urban settings for close on a hundred million years, developing and maintaining underground cities of specialised chambers and tunnels.

When we survey Mexico City, Tokyo, Los Angeles, we are amazed at what has been accomplished by humans. Yet Hoelldobler and Wilson’s magnificent work for ant lovers, The Ants, describes a supercolony of the ant Formica yessensis on the Ishikari Coast of Hokkaido. This ‘megalopolis’ was reported to be composed of 360 million workers and a million queens living in 4,500 interconnected nests across a territory of 2.7 square kilometres.

Such enduring and intricately meshed levels of technical achievement outstrip by far anything achieved by our distant ancestors. We hail as masterpieces the cave paintings in southern France and elsewhere, dating back some 20,000 years. Ant societies existed in something like their present form more than seventy million years ago. Beside this, prehistoric man looks technologically primitive. Is this then some kind of intelligence, albeit of a different kind?

Research conducted at Oxford, Sussex and Zürich Universities has shown that when desert ants return from a foraging trip, they navigate by integrating bearings and distances, which they continuously update in their heads. They combine the evidence of visual landmarks with a mental library of local directions, all within a framework which is consulted and updated. So ants can learn too.

And in a twelve-year programme of work, Ryabko and Reznikova have found evidence that ants can transmit very complex messages. Scouts who had located food in a maze returned to mobilise their foraging teams. They engaged in contact sessions, at the end of which the scout was removed in order to observe what her team might do. Often the foragers proceeded to the exact spot in the maze where the food had been. Elaborate precautions were taken to prevent the foraging team using odour clues. Discussion now centres on whether the route through the maze is communicated as a ‘left-right’ sequence of turns or as a ‘compass bearing and distance’ message.

During the course of this exhaustive study, Reznikova has grown so attached to her laboratory ants that she feels she knows them as individuals – even without the paint spots used to mark them. It’s no surprise that Edward Wilson, in his essay, ‘In the company of ants’, advises readers who ask what to do with the ants in their kitchen to: ‘Watch where you step. Be careful of little lives.’
